sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The 5 May 1990, Mw 5.8 earthquake took somewhat "by surprise" the Italian seismological community, due to its seemingly unexpected kinematics. In fact, its epicenter lies less than 25 km from the southern section of the causative fault of the Irpinia 1980 earthquake. The seismological data available for both events show that two very close sectors of the Southern Apennines behave quite differently - and at different depths. While the Irpinia fault is a large structure, down-throwing towards NE and with an almost pure normal faulting kinematics and developed throughout the first 12-13 kms (and outcropping), the Potenza structure is an almost pure strike-slip kinematics, running E-W, with right-lateral slip, and develops well below.
On the aftermath of the 31 Oct-1 Nov 2002, Molise earthquakes (Mw 5.8), it appeared that the seismogenic structures responsible for those events could be the western segments of the well known Mattinata fault. In fact, the Mattinata fault outcrops only 40 km to the east but its regional extent was certainly evident, since it runs through the entire Gargano promontory and shows a very long tectonic history. Furthermore, a very low stress drop suggested that those earthquakes had reactivated long-run faults, running in the lower portion of the seismogenic layer if compared with destructive events that took place in the core of the Southern Apennines.
Almost the same characteristics as above had been previously recognized for the Potenza events; the occurrence of the Molise sequence spurred an entirely new interest on the Potenza earthquake -including a novel interpretation.
Consequently, old and new data and literature allows to define a deeper seismogenic fault which can be the westerly expression of a longer, older regional structure, in a fashion comparable with the Mattinata -Molise 2002 fault system.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) What is the degree of interaction (if any) between the Irpinia 1980 fault and the Potenza 1990 fault? Do they need to really interact at some level?
2) Is the source of the 1990 earthquake really the southern "homologous" of the Molise 2002 events?
3) Is this Source really the westerly expression of a longer, regional E-W striking structure?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Azzara et al. (1993)
They recorded the seismic sequence immediately following the 5 May 1990, Potenza earthquake. They highlight that the more than 200 recorded aftershocks are located along a circa E-W striking, 20 km long lineament, and with hypocentral depths between 15 and 25 km. The authors remark that (a) these characteristics are quite uncommon in the Southern Apennines and (b) a 20 km long fault imaged by the aftershocks is quite long compared to the magnitude (Ml 5.2) of this earthquake.
Ekstrom (1994)
This Author analysed teleseismic data for the 1990 (Mw 5.7) and 1991 (Mw 5.2) Potenza earthquakes and shows focal mechanisms obtained by waveform inversion methods. Both events show strike-slip kinematics, occurring on a circa E-W trending plane.
Di Luccio et al. (2005)
They relocated the 1990-1991 Potenza sequences and calculated focal mechanisms. They noted that seismicity clusters along an E-W, dextral strike-slip structure. They also remark that second-order clusters are also present and reflect the activation of minor shears. In particular, these authors stress that the seismicity occurred within the basement of the subducting Apulian plate. They suggest that the E-W faults affecting the foreland region of Apennine propagate up to 25 km of depth. Also, they believe that (a) the Potenza earthquakes reflect the reactivation of a deep, preexisting fault system and (b) the seismotectonic setting of Apennines is characterized by NW-SE normal faults affecting the upper 15 km of the crust, and by E-W deeper strike-slip faults cutting the crystalline basement of the chain.
